item.title: Ketamine Restores Plasticity via AMPA Receptors
item.description: For the first time, scientists have visualized the molecular changes in the human brain that explain why ketamine works so quickly to treat depression.

item.title: Healing Without the Hallucinations: The Next Generation of Psilocybin Therapy
item.description: Scientists have synthesized a new compound that delivers the benefits of magic mushrooms without the mind-altering side effects.

item.title: Tubulin May Prevent Against Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s
item.description: Scientists discover that tubulin prevents brain disease by steering "troublemaker" proteins back to their healthy, productive roles.

item.title: Vision Rescued: How Stem Cells “Rehabilitate” the Dying Eye
item.description: New research reveals that transplanted stem cells act as a dynamic repair crew, preserving vision for the equivalent of 20 human years.

item.title: 70-Year-Old Drug Could Stop Epilepsy Seizures
item.description: Scientists discover that stabilizing a single ion transporter can flip the switch from seizure activity to healthy brain inhibition.

item.title: Brain’s Parenting Hub Redirects Care Toward Peers
item.description: New research reveals that our drive to help others is powered by the same brain circuits used for parenting.

item.title: Why Learning Makes Brain Cells Work Together, Not Apart
item.description: New research reveals that mastering a skill makes your brain cells act like a well-trained sports team rather than independent workers.

item.title: How the Brain Compensates for Sickle Cell Disease
item.description: Sickle cell disease causes the brain to rewire its executive and attention networks to compensate for low oxygen levels.

item.title: Why Millions Are Turning to ChatGPT for Mental Health
item.description: New research shows nearly half of UK adults are ready to use ChatGPT for counseling as a faster alternative to traditional mental health services.

item.title: Exhaustion Loophole: How Sleep Deprivation Compromises Justice
item.description: Sleep deprivation isn't just a minor variable—it's a threat to the truth. Scientists warn that exhausted suspects are more likely to confess to crimes they didn't commit.
